claim: Dnm2 deletion in developing Schwann cells resulted in severely impaired axonal sorting and myelination onset.
source: Dnm2 deletion in developing SCs resulted in severely impaired axonal sorting and myelination onset.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images showing impaired radial sorting and reduced myelinated fibers in P0-Dnm2KO mice at multiple developmental time points (Figure 1D-F), and by immunoblot data showing near absence of myelin proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Induced Dnm2 deletion in adult Schwann cells caused a rapidly-developing peripheral neuropathy with abundant demyelination.
source: Induced Dnm2 deletion in adult SCs caused a rapidly-developing peripheral neuropathy with abundant demyelination.
evidence: Supported by clinical assessments showing progressive motor impairment (Figure 2B,C), electron microscopy showing demyelinated axons at 6 wpT (Figure 2D,E), and electrophysiological measurements showing reduced motor nerve conduction velocity and conduction block (Figure 2H-J).

claim: Mutant Schwann cells underwent prominent cell death, at least partially due to cytokinesis failure.
source: In both experimental settings, mutant SCs underwent prominent cell death, at least partially due to cytokinesis failure.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing increased cleaved-caspase 3 positive Schwann cells (Figure 3E), live-cell imaging showing cytokinesis failures (Figure 4K), and increased multinucleated cells in culture (Figure 4H,I).

claim: When Dnm2 was deleted in adult Schwann cells, non-recombined Schwann cells still expressing DNM2 were able to remyelinate fast and efficiently, accompanied by neuropathy remission.
source: Strikingly, when Dnm2 was deleted in adult SCs, non-recombined SCs still expressing DNM2 were able to remyelinate fast and efficiently, accompanied by neuropathy remission.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy showing restoration of myelinated axons by 14 wpT (Figure 2D-F), clinical recovery data (Figure 2B), electrophysiological recovery (Figure 2H-J), and immunostaining showing loss of YFP-positive recombined cells with restoration of DNM2 expression (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claim: No major defects were found upon Dnm2 deletion in oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system.
source: In the central nervous system, however, we found no major defects upon Dnm2 deletion in oligodendrocytes.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing no significant differences in oligodendrocyte lineage cell numbers (Figure 5D,E), electron microscopy showing no detectable differences in myelinated axon numbers or myelin thickness (Figure 5F,G), and transferrin uptake assays showing no reduction in endocytosis (Figure 5C).

claim: DNM2 was substantially reduced in postnatal day 1 sciatic nerves of P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to control littermates.
source: We confirmed by immunoblotting that DNM2 was substantially reduced in postnatal day (P)1 sciatic nerves (SNs) of MpzCre:Dnm2loxP/loxP conditional knockout mice (termed P0-Dnm2KO) compared to control Dnm2loxP/loxP littermates (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing reduced DNM2 protein levels in P1 sciatic nerves (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Dnm2-deficient Schwann cells showed markedly reduced transferrin uptake.
source: Consistent with loss of DNM2 function, we found a markedly reduced transferrin uptake by Dnm2-deficient SCs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of transferrin uptake in primary Schwann cells showing reduced uptake in P0-Dnm2KO* cells compared to controls (Figure 1B).

claim: P0-Dnm2KO mice displayed pronounced clasping of their hind limbs by P24.
source: By P24, the mutants displayed also pronounced clasping of their hind limbs (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by tail-suspension test showing hind paw clasping phenotype (Figure 1C).

claim: At P1, there was a profound reduction in the numbers of myelinated axons in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to control littermates.
source: Already at P1, we found a profound reduction in the numbers of myelinated axons in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to control littermates (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification showing reduced myelinated fiber numbers (Figure 1D,E).

claim: The quantity of myelinated axons increased from P1 to P24 in control animals but remained almost undetectable in P0-Dnm2KO mice.
source: While the quantity of myelinated axons increased from P1 to P24 in control animals as expected, myelinated fibers remained almost undetectable in P0-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of myelinated fibers over developmental time points (Figure 1E).

claim: The myelin proteins P0, MAG, and MBP were nearly absent in P1 sciatic nerves of P0-Dnm2KO mice.
source: Consistent with these changes, the myelin proteins P0, MAG, and MBP were nearly absent in P1-SNs of P0-Dnm2KO (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing reduced levels of myelin proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: At P5, developing sciatic nerves of P0-Dnm2KO mice showed a strong increase in bundles containing axons with diameter larger than 1 μm compared to controls.
source: We counted the bundles that contained axons with a diameter larger than 1 μm (i.e. definitively destined for sorting and myelination) in SN cross-sections and found a strong increase in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of bundles with unsorted axons at P5 (Figure 1F).

claim: Developing sciatic nerves require DNM2 in Schwann cells for correct radial sorting of axons.
source: These data indicate that developing SNs require DNM2 in SCs for correct radial sorting of axons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased bundles with unsorted axons in P0-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 1F) and the profound reduction in myelinated axons (Figure 1D,E).

claim: P1 sciatic nerves of P0-Dnm2KO mice showed markedly increased amounts of cJUN and reduced KROX20 levels compared to controls.
source: These examinations revealed markedly increased amounts of cJUN and reduced KROX20 levels in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis of differentiation markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: DNM2 is needed for the molecular control of Schwann cell differentiation and the onset of myelination.
source: A plausible interpretation of these results is that DNM2 is needed for the molecular control of SC differentiation and the onset of myelination, although the changes might partially also reflect the observed delay in radial sorting.
evidence: Inferred from the altered expression of differentiation markers cJUN and KROX20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F) and the impaired myelination phenotype.

claim: DNM2 in Schwann cells is essential for accurate axonal radial sorting and subsequent myelination.
source: Taken together, our data show that DNM2 in SCs is essential for accurate axonal radial sorting and subsequent myelination.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple observations including impaired radial sorting (Figure 1F), reduced myelination (Figure 1D,E), and altered differentiation markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: At 4 weeks post-tamoxifen injection, DNM2 levels were reduced in sciatic nerves of P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls.
source: At 4 weeks post-tamoxifen injection (4 wpT), immunoblotting confirmed that DNM2 levels were reduced in SNs of MpzCreERT2:Dnm2loxP/loxP mice (P0ERT2-Dnm2KO) compared to controls (tamoxifen-injected Dnm2loxP/loxP mice) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing reduced DNM2 protein levels (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Approximately 30% of total Schwann cells were non-recombined in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
source: Residual DNM2 protein is likely due to non-recombined SCs that account for approximately 30% of total SCs as estimated by quantification of SOX10+ YFP+ recombined SCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), together with probable contributions by other DNM2-expressing cells located in SNs.
evidence: Supported by quantification of YFP-positive Schwann cells among total SOX10-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Induced P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice were behaviorally indistinguishable from controls up to 4 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Induced P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice were behaviorally indistinguishable from controls up to 4 wpT.
evidence: Supported by clinical assessment data showing no phenotype until 4 wpT (Figure 2B).

claim: After 4 weeks post-tamoxifen, P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutants started to show impaired righting responses, progressing to ataxic gait and finally to a moderate paraparesis at approximately 6 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: After 4 wpT, mutants started to show impaired righting responses, progressing to ataxic gait and finally to a moderate paraparesis at approximately 6 wpT (clinically assessed as described by King et al. (1983)) (Figure 2B,C—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by clinical assessment data showing progressive motor impairment (Figure 2B,C).

claim: All P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice improved rapidly after 6 weeks post-tamoxifen, reaching normal motor function again between 7 and 8 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Remarkably, all P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice improved rapidly thereafter, reaching normal motor function again between 7 wpT and 8 wpT (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by clinical assessment data showing recovery of motor function (Figure 2B).

claim: P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutant mice remained indistinguishable from control mice from 8 weeks post-tamoxifen until 41 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Subsequently, mutant mice remained indistinguishable from control mice until 41 wpT (last time point analyzed).
evidence: Supported by clinical assessment data showing sustained recovery (Figure 2B).

claim: Electrophysiological measurements revealed reduced motor nerve conduction velocities in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Electrophysiological measurements performed as schematized in Figure 2G revealed reduced motor nerve conduction velocities (mNCV) in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO at 6 wpT (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements showing reduced mNCV (Figure 2H,I).

claim: A severe conduction block was present in the nerves of P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: A severe conduction block was also present in the nerves of these mice as indicated by the almost complete absence of compound motor action potentials (CMAPs) when a proximal stimulus was applied (Figure 2H, red profile) and by the strongly reduced ratio between proximal and distal CAMPs (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements showing reduced proximal CMAP and reduced proximal to distal CMAP ratio (Figure 2H,J).

claim: Electrophysiological defects in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice were resolved by 14 weeks post-tamoxifen and remained at control levels until 41 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: These defects were resolved by 14 wpT and remained at control levels until 41 wpT, indicating that demyelination and subsequent remyelination are likely causes of the progressive clinical phenotype and its recovery in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements showing restoration of mNCV and CMAP ratios (Figure 2H-J).

claim: No detectable differences were evident between controls and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutants at 4 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: No detectable differences were evident between controls and mutants at 4 wpT (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification showing no differences in unmyelinated axons (Figure 2D,E).

claim: At 6 weeks post-tamoxifen, sciatic nerves of P0ERT2-Dnm2KO contained approximately 15% of demyelinated axons.
source: However, coinciding with the peak of motor impairment at 6 wpT, SNs of P0ERT2-Dnm2KO contained approximately 15% of demyelinated (i.e. myelination-competent but unmyelinated axons) (Figure 2D,E, black arrows; 14.91 ± 0.78 in mutant SNs versus none detected in control SNs; mean ±s.e.m.), rarely detected thinly remyelinated axons (Figure 2D, white arrowheads), and frequent immune cells such as macrophages (Figure 2D, black arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification showing demyelinated axons (Figure 2D,E).

claim: At 14 weeks post-tamoxifen, no demyelinated axons were found in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice and the number of myelinated axons reached control values.
source: Accordingly, at 14 wpT, we found no demyelinated axons (Figure 2D,E) and the number of myelinated axons reached control values (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification showing restoration of myelinated axon numbers (Figure 2D-F).

claim: Myelin sheaths were thinner after remyelination at 41 weeks post-tamoxifen in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
source: As described in other types of de- and remyelination, including in peripheral neuropathies of different types (Dyck and Thomas, 2005; Sanders and Whitteridge, 1946; Schröder, 1972; Stoll et al., 1986; Suter and Scherer, 2003), myelin sheaths were thinner after remyelination at 41 wpT also in our experimental setting (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), combined with shorter internodes as assessed at 14 wpT using teased nerve fiber preparations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by g-ratio measurements showing increased g-ratios (thinner myelin) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) and internode length measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), with reference to established literature on remyelination characteristics.

claim: Internodes were shorter at 14 weeks post-tamoxifen in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
source: As described in other types of de- and remyelination, including in peripheral neuropathies of different types (Dyck and Thomas, 2005; Sanders and Whitteridge, 1946; Schröder, 1972; Stoll et al., 1986; Suter and Scherer, 2003), myelin sheaths were thinner after remyelination at 41 wpT also in our experimental setting (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), combined with shorter internodes as assessed at 14 wpT using teased nerve fiber preparations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by internode length measurements from teased nerve fibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: An increase of cells strongly positive for P75NTR was found in sciatic nerves of P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutant mice at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen, followed by a decrease to virtually control levels by 14 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: By immunohistochemistry, we found an increase of cells that were strongly positive for P75NTR (CD271) in SNs of mutant mice at 6 wpT, followed by a decrease to virtually control levels by 14 wpT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of p75NTR signal intensity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claim: P75NTR transcript levels were increased in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves compared to controls at 4 weeks post-tamoxifen, together with Egr1 (Krox24) and cyclin D1.
source: Additionally, P75NTR transcript levels were increased in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO SNs compared to controls already at 4 wpT, together with other known molecules that are affected by dedifferentiation such as Egr1 (Krox24) and cyclin D1 (Ccnd1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis showing increased transcript levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).

claim: cJUN protein levels were prominently increased in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves compared to controls at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen and remained elevated up to 14 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: At 6 wpT, also cJUN protein levels were prominently increased in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO SNs compared to controls and remained elevated up to 14 wpT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing increased cJUN protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I).

claim: Loss of DNM2 in fully differentiated Schwann cells leads to a rapid but reversible demyelination, temporarily severely compromising peripheral nerve function.
source: Taken together, our results show that loss of DNM2 in fully differentiated SCs leads to a rapid but reversible demyelination, temporarily severely compromising peripheral nerve function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from clinical, electrophysiological, and morphological data showing demyelination followed by remyelination and functional recovery (Figure 2).

claim: DNM2 in Schwann cells is indispensable for myelin maintenance.
source: We conclude that DNM2 in SCs is indispensable for myelin maintenance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that induced deletion of DNM2 in adult Schwann cells leads to demyelination (Figure 2).

claim: 468 transcripts were jointly downregulated in both P0-Dnm2KO at P1 and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO at 4 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: We found 468 transcripts that were jointly downregulated and 1405 transcripts that were jointly upregulated in both P0-Dnm2KO and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutants (cutoff: 50% reduction or 50% increase compared to control levels, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data comparing transcriptomes (Figure 3A).

claim: 1405 transcripts were jointly upregulated in both P0-Dnm2KO at P1 and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO at 4 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: We found 468 transcripts that were jointly downregulated and 1405 transcripts that were jointly upregulated in both P0-Dnm2KO and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutants (cutoff: 50% reduction or 50% increase compared to control levels, FDR < 0.05) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data comparing transcriptomes (Figure 3A).

claim: Functions of the jointly downregulated genes were related to cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed that functions of the jointly downregulated genes were related to cholesterol biosynthesis (Figure 3A—source data 1), consistent with the reduced myelin content in mutant nerves (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing data (Figure 3A).

claim: The jointly upregulated gene set was enriched in genes associated with inflammatory responses.
source: The jointly upregulated set was enriched in genes associated with inflammatory responses, such as macrophage recruiting and/or stimulatory signals (Cd68, Csf1, Cd86, Mif, Cebpa), interleukins (Il1b, Il6), chemokines (Ccl2, Ccl3), and inflammatory cell markers (Ptprc (CD45)) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis and heat map of RNA-sequencing data (Figure 3A,B).

claim: Increased levels of transcripts associated with apoptosis were observed in Dnm2 knockout sciatic nerves.
source: We also noticed increased levels of transcripts associated with apoptosis (Figure 3B), including surface receptors that can mediate apoptotic signals (Fas, Tnfrsf1a, Tnfrsf10b), the death receptor adaptor Fadd, caspases (Casp1, Casp3, Casp4, Casp6, Casp8, Casp12), and caspase activator (Pycard).
evidence: Supported by heat map of RNA-sequencing data showing increased expression of apoptosis-related genes (Figure 3B).

claim: More CD45-positive inflammatory cells were detected in both P0-Dnm2KO and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls.
source: We detected more CD45+ inflammatory cells in both P0-Dnm2KO and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of CD45-positive cells (Figure 3C,D).

claim: During development, the number of immune cells was increased at P5 and P14 in P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves, progressing with age.
source: During development, the number of immune cells was increased at P5 and P14 in P0-Dnm2KO SNs, progressing with age (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of CD45-positive cells at different developmental time points (Figure 3C).

claim: In sciatic nerve maintenance, the highest number of CD45-positive cells was found at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
source: In SN maintenance, we found the highest number of CD45+ cells at 6 wpT (Figure 3D), concomitant with the peaking clinical phenotype and demyelination.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of CD45-positive cells at different time points (Figure 3D).

claim: Macrophages (CD68-positive) and T-cells (CD3-positive) were the prevalent populations of inflammatory cells in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
source: Macrophages (CD68+) and T-cells (CD3+) were the prevalent populations of inflammatory cells in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of CD68-positive and CD3-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Neutrophils and mast cells were also increased in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice, but to a lower extent than macrophages and T-cells.
source: Neutrophils and mast cells were also increased, but to a lower extent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of GR1-positive neutrophils and CD117-positive mast cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).

claim: Clodronate liposome treatment resulted in delayed functional recovery of P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutant mice.
source: This treatment resulted in delayed functional recovery of mutant mice, coherent with a beneficial role of macrophages in the speed of recovery (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by clinical assessment data comparing clodronate-treated and saline-treated P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Macrophages have a beneficial role in the speed of recovery in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice.
source: This treatment resulted in delayed functional recovery of mutant mice, coherent with a beneficial role of macrophages in the speed of recovery (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E—source data 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that macrophage depletion by clodronate liposomes delayed functional recovery (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).

claim: A robust increase in apoptotic Schwann cells was found in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls at P5 and P14.
source: In developing SNs, immunohistochemistry for cleaved-caspase 3 (cC3+) in combination with the SC marker SOX10, revealed a robust increase in apoptotic SCs in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls at P5 and P14 (Figure 3E), in agreement with the transcriptomics data.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of cleaved-caspase 3 positive SOX10-positive Schwann cells (Figure 3E).

claim: The total number of SOX10-positive Schwann cells per sciatic nerve cross-section at P5 was substantially reduced in P0-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls.
source: Analyses of the cellular composition of mutant SNs revealed a complex picture: the total number of SOX10+ SCs per SN cross-section at P5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) was substantially reduced compared to controls, despite the fact that the total number of DAPI+ nuclei was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), resulting in a decreased cellular proportion of SCs in P5 mutant nerves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SOX10-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: The total number of DAPI-positive nuclei was unaltered in P5 P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves compared to controls.
source: Analyses of the cellular composition of mutant SNs revealed a complex picture: the total number of SOX10+ SCs per SN cross-section at P5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) was substantially reduced compared to controls, despite the fact that the total number of DAPI+ nuclei was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), resulting in a decreased cellular proportion of SCs in P5 mutant nerves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of DAPI-positive nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

claim: There was a decreased cellular proportion of Schwann cells in P5 P0-Dnm2KO mutant nerves.
source: Analyses of the cellular composition of mutant SNs revealed a complex picture: the total number of SOX10+ SCs per SN cross-section at P5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) was substantially reduced compared to controls, despite the fact that the total number of DAPI+ nuclei was unaltered (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), resulting in a decreased cellular proportion of SCs in P5 mutant nerves (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by quantification showing reduced percentage of SOX10-positive cells among total DAPI-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).

claim: The number of SOX10-positive Schwann cells per sciatic nerve cross-section decreased between P5 and P14 in control mice.
source: As expected for controls, the number of SOX10+ SCs per SN cross-section decreased between P5 and P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SOX10-positive cells at P5 and P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: In P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves, the number of SOX10-positive Schwann cells remained similar between P5 and P14.
source: In P0-Dnm2KO SNs, however, the number of SOX10+ SCs remained similar between P5 and P14, while the number of total nuclei was robustly increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), as was the cross-sectional area of the mutant SNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SOX10-positive cells at P5 and P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: The number of total nuclei was robustly increased in P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves between P5 and P14.
source: In P0-Dnm2KO SNs, however, the number of SOX10+ SCs remained similar between P5 and P14, while the number of total nuclei was robustly increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), as was the cross-sectional area of the mutant SNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of DAPI-positive nuclei at P5 and P14 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

claim: The cross-sectional area of P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves was increased.
source: In P0-Dnm2KO SNs, however, the number of SOX10+ SCs remained similar between P5 and P14, while the number of total nuclei was robustly increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), as was the cross-sectional area of the mutant SNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of sciatic nerve endoneurial area (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).

claim: Putatively invading GLUT1-positive perineurial cells were found in P0-Dnm2KO mutants.
source: Additionally, we found putatively invading GLUT1+ perineurial cells by immunolabeling in mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of GLUT1-positive area (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E).

claim: Perineurial-like cells within the endoneurium were confirmed morphologically by electron microscopy in P14 P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves.
source: This finding was confirmed morphologically by EM analysis in P14 P0-Dnm2KO SNs (Figure 1D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images showing perineurial cells within the endoneurium (Figure 1D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).

claim: Perineurial-like cells within the endoneurium have been described previously if Schwann cells were reduced in numbers.
source: Such perineurial-like cells within the endoneurium have been described previously if SCs were reduced in numbers (Benninger et al., 2007; Grove et al., 2007; Jacob et al., 2011; Monk et al., 2011), or when SCs failed to secret DHH to allow correct maturation of the perineurium (Parmantier et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature describing similar observations.

claim: Increased levels of cleaved-caspase 3 protein were found in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen compared to controls.
source: In adult SNs, similarly to the developing SNs, we found increased levels of cleaved-caspase 3 protein in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice at 6 wpT compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing increased cleaved-caspase 3 protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D).

claim: Massive loss of recombined Schwann cells was observed in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO* mice.
source: These findings indicate elevated SC apoptosis, consistent with the massive loss of recombined SCs observed by staining for the recombination marker YFP in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO* mice (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing loss of YFP-positive cells (Figure 3F) and quantification (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Very few YFP-positive cells were left at 14 weeks post-tamoxifen in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO* mice.
source: Remarkably, very few YFP-positive cells were left at 14 wpT, in parallel with the observed recovery of the clinical phenotype.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing near absence of YFP-positive cells at 14 wpT (Figure 3F).

claim: Upon loss of DNM2, recombined Schwann cells undergo apoptosis, while non-recombined cells do not and are capable of remyelinating the sciatic nerve with high efficiency.
source: These results indicate that upon loss of DNM2, recombined SCs undergo apoptosis, while non-recombined cells do not and are capable of remyelinating the sciatic nerve with high efficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of YFP-positive cell loss (Figure 3F), increased apoptosis markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D), and restoration of myelination (Figure 2D-F).

claim: DNM2 expression was reduced in recombined YFP-positive Schwann cells at 4 weeks post-tamoxifen.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, DNM2 expression was reduced in recombined YFP-positive SCs at 4 wpT, while at 14 wpT, together with the loss of YFP-positive cells, SC expression of DNM2 was restored (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing reduced DNM2 in YFP-positive cells at 4 wpT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claim: At 14 weeks post-tamoxifen, together with the loss of YFP-positive cells, Schwann cell expression of DNM2 was restored.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, DNM2 expression was reduced in recombined YFP-positive SCs at 4 wpT, while at 14 wpT, together with the loss of YFP-positive cells, SC expression of DNM2 was restored (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing restoration of DNM2 expression at 14 wpT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claim: Both developing and adult Schwann cells depend critically on DNM2 for their survival.
source: Taken together, these results show that both developing and adult SCs depend critically on DNM2 for their survival and that, upon DNM2 loss, cells other than SCs invade developing peripheral nerves.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of increased apoptosis in both developmental and adult Dnm2 knockout models (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D).

claim: Upon DNM2 loss, cells other than Schwann cells invade developing peripheral nerves.
source: Taken together, these results show that both developing and adult SCs depend critically on DNM2 for their survival and that, upon DNM2 loss, cells other than SCs invade developing peripheral nerves.
evidence: Inferred from observations of increased inflammatory cells (Figure 3C,D) and GLUT1-positive perineurial cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D,E) in mutant nerves.

claim: Adult peripheral nerves have a remarkable plasticity allowing functional recovery after substantial Schwann cell loss.
source: Furthermore, our results indicate a remarkable plasticity of adult peripheral nerves allowing functional recovery after substantial SC loss.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice recovered functionally despite massive loss of recombined Schwann cells (Figure 2B, Figure 3F).

claim: The percentages of both EdU-positive and Ki-67-positive Schwann cells were substantially increased in P0-Dnm2KO sciatic nerves compared to controls at P5.
source: We found that the percentages of both EdU+ or Ki-67+ SCs (SOX10+) were substantially increased in P0-Dnm2KOsciatic nerves compared to controls at P5 (Figure 4B,C,D), indicating higher SC proliferation in mutants.
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling and Ki-67 immunostaining with quantification (Figure 4B,C,D).

claim: The proportion of EdU-positive among Ki-67-positive Schwann cells was increased in P0-Dnm2KO compared to controls at P5.
source: However, further analysis revealed that also the proportion of EdU+ among the Ki-67+ SCs was increased in P0-Dnm2KO compared to controls at P5 (Figure 4B,E), suggesting abnormal cell cycle progression.
evidence: Supported by quantification of EdU-positive cells among Ki-67-positive Schwann cells (Figure 4B,E).

claim: Dnm2KO Schwann cells may have defects in entering mitosis and/or during mitotic progression.
source: Since DNM2 has been mechanistically implicated in progression through the M phase and, in particular, in cytokinesis (Conery et al., 2010; Smith and Chircop, 2012; Thompson et al., 2002), we hypothesized that Dnm2KO SCs may have defects in entering mitosis and/or during mitotic progression.
evidence: Hypothesis based on established literature on DNM2 function in mitosis and cytokinesis, combined with observed abnormal cell cycle progression (Figure 4B,E).

claim: There was a decrease in Schwann cell mitotic events in Dnm2KO compared to control Schwann cells.
source: To investigate these aspects, live-cell imaging was carried out on YFP+ SCs isolated from P0-Dnm2KO* and control* mice at P1. We found a decrease in SC mitotic events in Dnm2KO compared to control SCs (Figure 4F), associated with an increase in mitosis duration in Dnm2KO SCs (Figure 4G,J).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging and quantification of mitotic events (Figure 4F,J).

claim: There was an increase in mitosis duration in Dnm2KO Schwann cells.
source: To investigate these aspects, live-cell imaging was carried out on YFP+ SCs isolated from P0-Dnm2KO* and control* mice at P1. We found a decrease in SC mitotic events in Dnm2KO compared to control SCs (Figure 4F), associated with an increase in mitosis duration in Dnm2KO SCs (Figure 4G,J).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging and quantification of mitosis duration (Figure 4G,J).

claim: Mutant Schwann cells were more often multinucleated compared to controls at both 48 and 72 hours after isolation.
source: Additionally, mutant cells were more often multinucleated compared to controls, at both 48 and 72 hr after isolation (Figure 4H,I), likely as a result of impaired cytokinesis.
evidence: Supported by quantification of multinucleated cells in culture (Figure 4H,I).

claim: Failures in cytokinesis were documented in Dnm2KO mutant Schwann cells.
source: Indeed, we could document failures in cytokinesis in mutant cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging showing cytokinesis failure (Figure 4K).

claim: Together with ensuring Schwann cell survival, DNM2 in Schwann cells is necessary to ensure proper cell cycle progression, mitotic entry, and cytokinesis.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that, together with ensuring SC survival, DNM2 in SCs is necessary to ensure proper cell cycle progression, mitotic entry, and cytokinesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of abnormal cell cycle markers (Figure 4B-E), reduced mitotic events, increased mitosis duration (Figure 4F,G,J), increased multinucleated cells (Figure 4H,I), and cytokinesis failures (Figure 4K).

claim: DNM2 was effectively reduced in spinal cords from CNP-Dnm2KO compared to control littermates at P14 and P60.
source: First, we determined by immunoblotting that DNM2 was effectively reduced in spinal cords from CNP-Dnm2KO compared to control littermates (P14, P60) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing reduced DNM2 protein levels in spinal cord (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Mutant CC1-positive oligodendrocytes showed no detectable specific staining for DNM2 in CNP-Dnm2KO mice at P14.
source: To confirm depletion of DNM2 in mature OLs, we co-stained P14 spinal cord sections from CNP-Dnm2KO and control mice for DNM2 and the marker CC1. As expected and contrary to controls, mutant CC1+ OLs showed no detectable specific staining for DNM2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing absence of DNM2 in CC1-positive oligodendrocytes (Figure 5B).

claim: Transferrin uptake was not detectably reduced in Dnm2KO oligodendrocyte lineage cells.
source: Analogous to the previous experiments with DNM2-deficient SCs, we then assessed the effect of loss of DNM2 function by measuring transferrin uptake using primary OL lineage cells isolated from brain of control* and CNP-Dnm2KO* mice (carrying also the Cre-dependent Rosa26-YFP reporter allele) at P7 and cultured for 14 days. In contrast to our findings in SCs, transferrin uptake was not detectably reduced in Dnm2KO OL lineage cells (Figure 5C), despite an effective decrease of DNM2 levels as determined by immunoblotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of transferrin uptake showing no difference between control and CNP-Dnm2KO oligodendrocyte lineage cells (Figure 5C).

claim: No significant differences were found between control and CNP-Dnm2KO mice in the number of total oligodendrocyte lineage cells, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells, or mature oligodendrocytes in spinal cord, corpus callosum, and cerebellar white matter at P14.
source: We then assessed the impact of DNM2 loss on OL development and differentiation by analyzing OL lineage cell numbers and differentiation markers in multiple CNS regions at P14, including spinal cord, corpus callosum, and cerebellar white matter lobes IV-V. No significant differences were found between control and CNP-Dnm2KO mice in the number of total OL lineage cells (OLIG2+), oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs; PDGFRα+ OLIG2+), or mature OLs (CC1+ OLIG2+) in all regions analyzed (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification of oligodendrocyte lineage cell markers (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claim: No detectable differences were found in the number of myelinated axons or in myelin thickness (g-ratio) in the spinal cord ventral white matter (P14, P60) and the corpus callosum (P60) of CNP-Dnm2KO mice compared to controls.
source: We further examined CNS myelination in CNP-Dnm2KO and control littermates by electron microscopy (Figure 5F). No detectable differences were found in the number of myelinated axons or in myelin thickness (g-ratio) in the spinal cord ventral white matter (P14, P60) and the corpus callosum (P60) (Figure 5F,G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images and quantification of myelinated axons and g-ratios (Figure 5F,G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: DNM2 is largely dispensable for oligodendrocyte differentiation and CNS myelination.
source: Overall our observations indicate that DNM2 is largely dispensable for OL differentiation and CNS myelination, in contrast to the essential role of DNM2 in SCs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the absence of detectable defects in oligodendrocyte numbers, differentiation markers, and myelination in CNP-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 5).

claim: Compensatory functional mechanisms, potentially including other isoforms of dynamins, may contribute to the lack of oligodendrocyte defects upon DNM2 deletion.
source: Compensatory functional mechanisms, potentially including other isoforms of dynamins, may contribute to these findings.
evidence: Speculation based on the absence of oligodendrocyte defects despite DNM2 deletion, considering that other dynamin isoforms are expressed in oligodendrocytes.

claim: Subtle effects of lack of DNM2 on oligodendrocyte differentiation or on important earlier functions of DNM2 in oligodendrocyte lineage development may not have been detected due to potential experimental limitations.
source: However, we can also not exclude subtle effects of lack of DNM2 on OL differentiation (or on important earlier functions of DNM2 in OL lineage development) that we may not have detected due to potential experimental limitations.
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential experimental limitations in detecting subtle effects.

claim: Developing Schwann cells require the specific functions of DNM2 for radial sorting of large caliber axons and their subsequent myelination.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that developing SCs require the specific functions of the large GTPase DNM2 for radial sorting of large caliber axons and their subsequent myelination.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of impaired radial sorting and myelination in P0-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 1).

claim: DNM2 in Schwann cells is essential for myelin maintenance.
source: In addition, we show that DNM2 in SCs is also essential for myelin maintenance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of demyelination upon induced deletion of DNM2 in adult Schwann cells (Figure 2).

claim: Lack of DNM2 in developing or adult Schwann cells resulted in a severe peripheral neuropathy, characterized by Schwann cell loss and signs of inflammation.
source: Using loxP/Cre recombination-mediated gene ablation in mice, we found that lack of DNM2 in developing or adult SCs resulted in a severe peripheral neuropathy, characterized by SC loss and signs of inflammation.
evidence: Supported by observations of clinical phenotypes, Schwann cell apoptosis, and inflammatory cell infiltration in both P0-Dnm2KO and P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice (Figures 1-3).

claim: Removal of DNM2 specifically from adult Schwann cells induced fast demyelination, coupled with Schwann cell dedifferentiation and ensued by widespread apoptosis of recombined DNM2-deficient Schwann cells.
source: Removal of DNM2 specifically from adult SCs induced fast demyelination, coupled with SC dedifferentiation and ensued by widespread apoptosis of recombined DNM2-deficient SCs.
evidence: Supported by observations of demyelination (Figure 2D,E), dedifferentiation markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I), and loss of YFP-positive recombined cells (Figure 3F).

claim: This striking Schwann cell loss was rapidly compensated for by a minor fraction of non-recombined DNM2-expressing Schwann cells, paralleled by complete functional recovery of the animals within two weeks after the peak of symptoms.
source: Remarkably, this striking cell loss was rapidly compensated for by a minor fraction of non-recombined DNM2-expressing SCs, paralleled by complete functional recovery of the animals within two weeks after the peak of symptoms.
evidence: Supported by observations of clinical recovery (Figure 2B), restoration of myelination (Figure 2D-F), and persistence of non-recombined DNM2-expressing Schwann cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claim: DNM2 is crucial for Schwann cell survival and differentiation, both in development and in adulthood.
source: At the cellular level, our data indicate that DNM2 is crucial for SC survival and differentiation, both in development and in adulthood, and acts as a prominent regulator of the cell cycle.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of increased apoptosis (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D), altered differentiation markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I), and cell cycle defects (Figure 4).

claim: DNM2 acts as a prominent regulator of the cell cycle in Schwann cells.
source: At the cellular level, our data indicate that DNM2 is crucial for SC survival and differentiation, both in development and in adulthood, and acts as a prominent regulator of the cell cycle.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of abnormal cell cycle progression, reduced mitotic events, increased mitosis duration, and cytokinesis failures (Figure 4).

claim: The intimate dependency of Schwann cells on DNM2 is consistent with a particular susceptibility of these cells to neuropathy-associated DNM2 mutations.
source: The intimate dependency of SCs on DNM2 is consistent with a particular susceptibility of these cells to neuropathy-associated DNM2 mutations.
evidence: Inference based on the observed essential role of DNM2 in Schwann cells and the known association of DNM2 mutations with peripheral neuropathy.

claim: No evidence was found supporting the hypothesis that DNM2 is necessary for oligodendrocyte-mediated CNS myelination.
source: Triggered by the observed severe consequences of DNM2 deficiency in peripheral myelinating glia, we examined also whether DNM2 is necessary for OL in CNS myelination. However, we found no evidence supporting this hypothesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the absence of detectable defects in oligodendrocyte differentiation and CNS myelination in CNP-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 5).

claim: Reduced Schwann cell proliferation is correlated with incomplete radial sorting in mouse models.
source: Reduced SC proliferation is correlated with incomplete radial sorting in mouse models (Benninger et al., 2007; Berti et al., 2011; Brinkmann et al., 2008; Grove et al., 2007; Porrello et al., 2014), and excessive apoptosis can lead to a similar outcome (Jacob et al., 2011; Messing et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Excessive apoptosis can lead to incomplete radial sorting.
source: Reduced SC proliferation is correlated with incomplete radial sorting in mouse models (Benninger et al., 2007; Berti et al., 2011; Brinkmann et al., 2008; Grove et al., 2007; Porrello et al., 2014), and excessive apoptosis can lead to a similar outcome (Jacob et al., 2011; Messing et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dual regulation of proliferation and apoptosis can allow cells to reach a new equilibrium that remains compatible with proper sorting.
source: In some cases, dual regulation of proliferation and apoptosis allows cells to reach a new equilibrium that remains compatible with proper sorting (D'Antonio et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased Schwann cell proliferation and survival can accelerate radial sorting.
source: Increased SC proliferation and survival can instead accelerate radial sorting (Figlia et al., 2017; Grigoryan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: After DNM2 deletion in developing Schwann cells, mutant sciatic nerves contained fewer Schwann cells compared to controls at P5, concomitant with increased apoptosis and impaired radial sorting.
source: We found that after DNM2 deletion in developing SCs, mutant SNs contained fewer SCs compared to controls at P5, concomitant with increased apoptosis and impaired radial sorting.
evidence: Supported by quantification of SOX10-positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), cleaved-caspase 3 positive cells (Figure 3E), and bundles with unsorted axons (Figure 1F).

claim: Increased apoptosis could explain the reduced number of Schwann cells in P0-Dnm2KO mice, especially if not counteracted by higher levels of proliferation.
source: This increased apoptosis could explain the reduced number of SCs, especially if not counteracted by higher levels of proliferation.
evidence: Inference based on the observed increased apoptosis (Figure 3E) and reduced Schwann cell numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).

claim: Dnm2KO Schwann cells are affected at various stages of the cell cycle, including impaired entry into the mitotic phase, longer duration of the mitotic process until complete cell division, and fewer mitotic events completed in the same time frame as in control Schwann cells.
source: Subsequent experiments revealed that Dnm2KO SCs are affected at various stages of the cell cycle, including 1) impaired entry into the mitotic phase, 2) longer duration of the mitotic process until complete cell division, which translated into 3) fewer mitotic events completed in the same time frame as in control SCs.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging showing reduced mitotic events (Figure 4F) and increased mitosis duration (Figure 4G,J).

claim: Dnm2KO Schwann cells were more prone to cytokinesis failure compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, Dnm2KO SCs were more prone to cytokinesis failure compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging showing cytokinesis failures (Figure 4K) and increased multinucleated cells (Figure 4H,I).

claim: DNM2 has been previously implicated in cytokinesis.
source: DNM2 has been previously implicated in cytokinesis (Smith and Chircop, 2012), and our evidence is coherent with such a role also in SCs.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature and observations of cytokinesis failures in Dnm2KO Schwann cells (Figure 4K).

claim: Cytokinesis failure, with the consequent formation of multinucleated cells, likely contributes to apoptosis and ultimately the decrease in Schwann cell numbers in P0-Dnm2KO mice at P5.
source: It is likely that cytokinesis failure, with the consequent formation of multinucleated cells, contributes to apoptosis and ultimately the decrease in SC numbers in P0-Dnm2KO mice at P5, analogous to observations made in other cell types (Chircop et al., 2011; Conery et al., 2010; Joshi et al., 2011; Redgrove et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference based on observations of cytokinesis failures (Figure 4K), multinucleated cells (Figure 4H,I), increased apoptosis (Figure 3E), and reduced Schwann cell numbers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), with reference to similar observations in other cell types.

claim: Successful radial sorting is dependent on coordinated Schwann cell cytoskeletal rearrangements in order to extend processes that reach axons and establish stable interaction required for the following myelination step.
source: Besides appropriate cell number expansion, successful radial sorting is dependent on coordinated SC cytoskeletal rearrangements in order to extend processes that reach axons and establish stable interaction required for the following myelination step.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about radial sorting mechanisms.

claim: Alterations in stability and dynamic arrangements of actin filaments or microtubules affect Schwann cell process extension and radial sorting and/or myelination.
source: Alterations in stability and dynamic arrangements of actin filaments or microtubules affect SC process extension and radial sorting (Grove et al., 2007; Sparrow et al., 2012) and/or myelination (Jin et al., 2011; Novak et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNM2 is involved in regulating actin and microtubule dynamics and stability.
source: Since DNM2 is involved in regulating actin and microtubule dynamics and stability (Gu et al., 2010; Tanabe and Takei, 2009; Yamada et al., 2016), potential cytoskeleton abnormalities in P0-Dnm2KO SCs may also partially contribute to the impaired radial sorting phenotype.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Potential cytoskeleton abnormalities in P0-Dnm2KO Schwann cells may partially contribute to the impaired radial sorting phenotype.
source: Since DNM2 is involved in regulating actin and microtubule dynamics and stability (Gu et al., 2010; Tanabe and Takei, 2009; Yamada et al., 2016), potential cytoskeleton abnormalities in P0-Dnm2KO SCs may also partially contribute to the impaired radial sorting phenotype.
evidence: Speculation based on known functions of DNM2 in cytoskeletal regulation and observed radial sorting defects.

claim: Once an axon segment is sorted from the bundle, the associated pro-myelinating Schwann cell undergoes extensive transcriptional changes, generally characterized by shutdown of proliferation-related (myelin-suppressing) transcripts, and upregulation of the myelination program chiefly driven by key transcription factor KROX20.
source: Once an axon segment is sorted from the bundle, the associated pro-myelinating SC undergoes extensive transcriptional changes, generally characterized by shutdown of proliferation-related (myelin-suppressing) transcripts, and upregulation of the myelination program chiefly driven by key transcription factor KROX20 (Decker et al., 2006; Topilko et al., 1994).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge with citations to previous literature.

claim: The processes of Schwann cell radial sorting, proliferation and ensuing differentiation/myelination are closely linked.
source: Thus, the processes of SC radial sorting, proliferation and ensuing differentiation/myelination are closely linked.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about Schwann cell development.

claim: Imbalances in the expression of opposing differentiation regulators cJUN and KROX20 can negatively influence Schwann cell differentiation.
source: Such imbalances on the expression of opposing differentiation regulators can negatively influence SC differentiation (Parkinson et al., 2008), consistent with the interpretation of impaired SC differentiation at the onset of myelination as an additional consequence of DNM2 deficiency.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature and observations of altered cJUN and KROX20 levels in P0-Dnm2KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).

claim: DNM2 is widely associated with clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: DNM2 is widely associated with clathrin-mediated endocytosis which we found to be strongly reduced in DNM2KO SCs.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and supported by transferrin uptake assay showing reduced endocytosis (Figure 1B).

claim: DNM2-based control mechanisms of Schwann cell radial sorting and differentiation may include regulation of endocytosis and recycling of cell surface proteins such as ErbB2/ErbB3-, integrin β1-, and GPR126-receptors.
source: Thus, DNM2-based control mechanisms of SC radial sorting and differentiation may also include regulation of endocytosis and recycling of cell surface proteins such as ErbB2/ErbB3-, integrin β1-, and GPR126-receptors.
evidence: Speculation based on known functions of DNM2 in endocytosis and the known roles of these receptors in Schwann cell development.

claim: ErbB2/ErbB3-, integrin β1-, and GPR126-receptors have been previously implicated in Schwann cell radial sorting.
source: These proteins have been previously implicated in SC radial sorting (Feltri et al., 2016) and can be internalized via DNM2-dependent endocytosis (Paul et al., 2015; Sorkin and Goh, 2009a; Sorkin and von Zastrow, 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ErbB2/ErbB3-, integrin β1-, and GPR126-receptors can be internalized via DNM2-dependent endocytosis.
source: These proteins have been previously implicated in SC radial sorting (Feltri et al., 2016) and can be internalized via DNM2-dependent endocytosis (Paul et al., 2015; Sorkin and Goh, 2009a; Sorkin and von Zastrow, 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An impact of DNM2-mediated internalization on surface receptors is indirectly supported by studies in cell culture, showing that expression of a neuropathy-associated DNM2 mutant alters surface levels of integrin β1 and ErbB2.
source: Furthermore, an impact of DNM2-mediated internalization on surface receptors (potentially also altering signaling) is indirectly supported by studies in cell culture, showing that expression of a neuropathy-associated DNM2 mutant alters surface levels of integrin β1 and ErbB2 (Sidiropoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In adult nerves, Schwann cells remain strictly dependent on the continuous action of transcriptional regulators to preserve myelin maintenance.
source: In adult nerves, SCs remain strictly dependent on the continuous action of transcriptional regulators to preserve myelin maintenance (Bremer et al., 2011; Brügger et al., 2015; Decker et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNM2 function is essential in adult Schwann cells to maintain myelination.
source: We found that also DNM2 function is essential in adult SCs to maintain myelination.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of demyelination upon induced deletion of DNM2 in adult Schwann cells (Figure 2).

claim: Induced loss of DNM2 specifically in adult Schwann cells evoked an acute and robust demyelination, accompanied by clinical neuropathy and coupled with Schwann cell dedifferentiation and invasion of inflammatory cells.
source: Induced loss of DNM2 specifically in adult SCs evoked an acute and robust demyelination, accompanied by clinical neuropathy and coupled with SC dedifferentiation and invasion of inflammatory cells.
evidence: Supported by observations of demyelination (Figure 2D,E), clinical phenotype (Figure 2B,C), dedifferentiation markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-I), and inflammatory cell infiltration (Figure 3D).

claim: Schwann cell dedifferentiation was followed by progressive loss of the recombined DNM2-negative Schwann cell pool (approximately 70% of all Schwann cells originally present).
source: SC dedifferentiation was followed by progressive loss of the recombined DNM2-negative SC pool (i.e. approx. 70% of all SCs originally present).
evidence: Supported by observations of YFP-positive cell loss (Figure 3F) and quantification showing approximately 70% recombination efficiency (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).

claim: Despite the prominent pathology developed in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO nerves and the widespread loss of Schwann cells, there was robust histological and functional recovery.
source: Despite the prominent pathology developed in these nerves and the widespread loss of SCs, there was robust histological and functional recovery.
evidence: Supported by observations of clinical recovery (Figure 2B), restoration of myelination (Figure 2D-F), and electrophysiological recovery (Figure 2H-J).

claim: Recovery in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mice was mediated by Schwann cells that did not lose DNM2 (approximately 30% of the original Schwann cell pool).
source: This recovery was mediated by SCs that did not lose DNM2 in our experimental system (i.e. approx. 30% of the original SC pool).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that approximately 30% of Schwann cells were non-recombined (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) and that DNM2 expression was restored at 14 wpT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).

claim: The results demonstrate an astonishing ability of adult mouse peripheral nerves to repair damage if faced by massive Schwann cell death and demyelination.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate an astonishing ability of adult mouse peripheral nerves to repair damage if faced by massive SC death and demyelination.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of functional and histological recovery despite massive Schwann cell loss (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Demyelination and dedifferentiation of Schwann cells, coupled with low grade invasion of inflammatory cells, are common features of acquired and inherited peripheral neuropathies.
source: These findings may also have significant overtones for our understanding of human nerve diseases since demyelination and dedifferentiation of SCs, coupled with low grade invasion of inflammatory cells, are common features of acquired and inherited peripheral neuropathies (Martini and Willison, 2016).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge with citation to previous literature.

claim: If prominent reparative mechanisms are sufficiently effective, secondary axonal damage might be limited or prevented allowing efficient recovery.
source: One might speculate that if such prominent reparative mechanisms as observed in our model are sufficiently effective, secondary axonal damage might be limited or prevented allowing efficient recovery.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed recovery in the experimental model.

claim: Fostering the intrinsic regenerative capability of Schwann cells might be a promising therapeutic target in acquired neuropathies and/or in hereditary neuropathies, including in some forms of CMT where this process might be chronically reduced due to genetic mutations.
source: Thus, fostering the intrinsic regenerative capability of SCs might be a promising therapeutic target in acquired neuropathies and/or in hereditary neuropathies, including in some forms of CMT where this process might be chronically reduced due to genetic mutations.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed regenerative capability in the experimental model and its potential therapeutic implications.

claim: It cannot be determined currently to which extent the observed regenerative capability in P0ERT2-Dnm2KO mutants may include the participation/recruitment of non-myelinating Schwann cells that are normally associated with Remak bundles.
source: Of note, we cannot determine currently to which extent the observed regenerative capability in our mutants may include the participation/recruitment of non-myelinating Schwann cells that are normally associated with Remak bundles (Murinson et al., 2005).
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitation with citation to relevant literature.

claim: Contributions of progenitors turning into Schwann cells in the experimental setting cannot be excluded.
source: Similarly, we cannot exclude contributions of progenitors turning into SCs in our experimental setting (Petersen and Adameyko, 2017; Stierli et al., 2018).
evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitation with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Myelination in the PNS and CNS encompasses numerous similarities and yet striking differences, including the cell types that perform this function, the structure and composition of the myelin they produce, and the molecular pathways that govern myelination and homeostasis of the axon-myelin unit.
source: Myelination in the PNS and CNS encompasses numerous similarities and yet striking differences, including the cell types that perform this function, the structure and composition of the myelin they produce, and the molecular pathways that govern myelination and homeostasis of the axon-myelin unit.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about myelination in PNS and CNS.

claim: Previous in vitro experiments suggested that in oligodendrocytes, dynamins contribute to myelin protein re-localization, allowing plasma membrane specialization and possibly affecting myelination.
source: Previous in vitro experiments suggested that in OLs, dynamins contribute to myelin protein re-localization, allowing plasma membrane specialization and possibly affecting myelination.
evidence: Draws from previous literature on oligodendrocyte studies.

claim: Previous experiments using overexpression of dominant-negative forms of DNM2 or chemical antagonists may have caused unintended gain-of-function effects or lacked complete specificity.
source: These experiments used overexpression of dominant-negative forms of DNM2, which may have caused some unintended gain-of-function effects, or chemical antagonists which may not have been completely specific (Trajkovic et al., 2006; Winterstein et al., 2008).
evidence: Critical evaluation of previous experimental approaches with citations to relevant literature.

claim: It appears likely that unexplored compensatory mechanisms, possibly including other DNM isoforms, substitute for DNM2 functions in oligodendrocytes in vivo.
source: It appears likely that unexplored compensatory mechanisms, possibly including other DNM isoforms, substitute for DNM2 functions in OL in vivo.
evidence: Speculation based on the absence of oligodendrocyte defects despite DNM2 deletion.

claim: DNM2 in Schwann cells is essential for proper peripheral nerve development and myelin maintenance.
source: In conclusion, our study shows that DNM2 in SCs is essential for proper peripheral nerve development and myelin maintenance.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations in both developmental and adult Dnm2 knockout models (Figures 1 and 2).

claim: Schwann cells are dependent on DNM2 for clathrin-mediated endocytosis, cell cycle progression and cytokinesis, differentiation, myelination, and maintenance of the myelinated state in adult mice.
source: The key findings highlight that SCs are dependent on DNM2 for clathrin-mediated endocytosis, cell cycle progression and cytokinesis, differentiation, myelination, and maintenance of the myelinated state in adult mice.
evidence: Summary of key findings supported by data from multiple experiments (Figures 1-4).

claim: Specific DNM2 functions in oligodendrocytes are largely dispensable for CNS myelination, in line with the PNS-specific defects of CMT-causing DNM2 mutations.
source: In contrast, specific DNM2 functions in OL are largely dispensable for CNS myelination, in line with the PNS-specific defects of CMT-causing DNM2 mutations.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the absence of oligodendrocyte defects (Figure 5) and known clinical features of DNM2-associated CMT.

claim: Elimination of DNM2 in Schwann cells of adult mice caused widespread Schwann cell death.
source: Elimination of DNM2 in SCs of adult mice caused widespread SC death.
evidence: Supported by observations of YFP-positive cell loss (Figure 3F) and increased apoptosis markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D).

claim: Experiments with induced DNM2 deletion in adult Schwann cells revealed an astonishing self-healing capability of peripheral nerves when affected by massive Schwann cell death and demyelination.
source: Remarkably, these experiments revealed an astonishing self-healing capability of peripheral nerves when affected by massive SC death and demyelination.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from observations of functional and histological recovery despite massive Schwann cell loss (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Fostering the highly efficient regenerative process underlying peripheral nerve recovery is an appealing target for future therapeutic approaches in selected peripheral nerve diseases.
source: Fostering the underlying highly efficient regenerative process is an appealing target for future therapeutic approaches in selected peripheral nerve diseases.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed regenerative capability and its potential therapeutic implications.

claim: Complete loss of DNM2 in mice results in early embryonic lethality.
source: Complete loss of DNM2 in mice results in early embryonic lethality (Ferguson et al., 2009), highlighting the crucial importance of DNM2 in development.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Specific ablation of Dnm2 in mouse skeletal muscle resulted in muscle fiber atrophy and loss, lipid droplet accumulation, mitochondrial aberrations, defective neuromuscular junctions, and peripheral nerve degeneration.
source: These studies include specific ablation of Dnm2 in mouse skeletal muscle, which resulted in muscle fiber atrophy and loss, lipid droplet accumulation, mitochondrial aberrations, defective neuromuscular junctions, and peripheral nerve degeneration (Tinelli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In lymphocytes, loss of Dnm2 led to reduced proliferation, triggered by reduced T-cell receptor endocytosis and decreased mTORC1 signaling.
source: In lymphocytes, loss of Dnm2 led to reduced proliferation, triggered by reduced T-cell receptor endocytosis and decreased mTORC1 signaling (Willinger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the megakaryocyte lineage, Dnm2 deletion delayed megakaryocyte maturation in the bone marrow, resulting in macrothrombocytopenia and a reduction in circulating platelet cells.
source: In the megakaryocyte lineage, Dnm2 deletion delayed megakaryocyte maturation in the bone marrow, resulting in macrothrombocytopenia and a reduction in circulating platelet cells (Bender et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In germline cells, Dnm2 ablation caused male sterility due to cell cycle arrest, increased cell death, and reduced proliferation.
source: In germline cells, Dnm2 ablation caused male sterility due to cell cycle arrest, increased cell death, and reduced proliferation (Redgrove et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Specific ablation of Dnm2 did not affect neuronal development in the auditory brainstem, but it exacerbated defects of Dnm1-Dnm3 double knockout mice.
